answer_text:
# 🟣 The History of Purple

---

## A Colour Born from the Sea

Of all the colours that have shaped human history, none has wielded more power, provoked more obsession, or cost more lives than **purple**. Its story begins not in a painter's studio or a philosopher's study, but on the rocky shores of the ancient Mediterranean, in the stinking, sun-baked workshops of a seafaring people.

As early as the 15th century BC, the citizens of Sidon and Tyre, two cities on the coast of Ancient Phoenicia (present-day Lebanon), were producing purple dye from a sea snail. It has even been suggested that the name "Phoenicia" itself means *'land of purple.'* The secret of how to make this magical colour was closely kept, but the ancient Phoenicians made it famous as they roamed, raided, traded and colonised the coastlines and islands of the ancient Mediterranean Sea.

The dye was known as **Tyrian purple**, and its production was nothing short of laborious — and deeply unpleasant. To harvest it, dye-makers had to crack open the snail's shell, extract a purple-producing mucus, and expose it to sunlight for a precise amount of time. In the sunlight, the juice turned white, then yellow-green, then green, then violet, then a red that turned darker and darker. The process had to be stopped at exactly the right moment to obtain the desired colour, which could range from a bright crimson to a dark purple, the colour of dried blood.

The quantities required were staggering. It could take up to 12,000 mollusks to produce just 1 gram of dye. Mountains of empty shells have been found at the ancient sites of Sidon and Tyre.

---

## The Colour of Gods and Emperors

The dye was greatly prized in antiquity because the colour did not easily fade, but instead became *brighter* with weathering and sunlight. It came in various shades, the most prized being that of black-tinted clotted blood.

Because it was extremely tedious to make, Tyrian purple was expensive: the 4th-century BC historian Theopompus reported, "Purple for dyes fetched its weight in silver at Colophon" in Asia Minor. Such an extraordinary price made purple not merely a colour but a declaration of rank. Tyrian purple became the colour of kings, nobles, priests and magistrates all around the Mediterranean and Europe. It was mentioned in the Old Testament — in the Book of Exodus — and also in both the *Iliad* of Homer and the *Aeneid* of Virgil. Alexander the Great, the basileus of the Seleucid Empire, and the kings of Ptolemaic Egypt all wore Tyrian purple.

In Rome, the colour took on an almost divine authority. The most senior Roman magistrates wore a *toga praetexta*, a white toga edged in Tyrian purple. The even more sumptuous *toga picta*, solid Tyrian purple with gold thread edging, was worn by generals celebrating a Roman triumph. During the Roman Empire, purple was more and more associated exclusively with the emperors and their officers. The Emperor Caligula had the King of Mauritania murdered for wearing a purple mantle better than his own, and Nero made it punishable by death for anyone else to wear the colour.

---

## Born in the Purple

No civilisation clung to purple with more ferocity than the **Byzantine Empire**. Through the early Christian era, the rulers of the Byzantine Empire continued the use of purple as the imperial colour, for diplomatic gifts, and even for imperial documents and the pages of the Bible. Gospel manuscripts were written in gold lettering on parchment that was coloured Tyrian purple. Empresses gave birth in the Purple Chamber, and the emperors born there were known as "born to the purple," to separate them from emperors who won or seized the title through political intrigue or military force.

Purple also came to represent spirituality and holiness because the ancient emperors, kings and queens who wore the colour were often thought of as gods or descendants of the gods.

"Purple was a status symbol for the Roman emperors and the powerful representatives of the emergent power, the Catholic Church," says Maria Melo of NOVA University at Lisbon, a conservation scientist who studies ancient dyes.

In western Europe, the Emperor Charlemagne was crowned in 800 wearing a mantle of Tyrian purple, and was buried in 814 in a shroud of the same colour.

Then, abruptly, it ended. After the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, the colour lost its imperial status.

---

## The Tudor Stranglehold

Purple did not disappear from the courts of Europe — it merely migrated westward. In Elizabethan Europe, purple was reserved for royalty, and throughout England's Tudor period only King Henry VIII was allowed to dress in the colour; he went as far as committing an Earl to death by treason for wearing it. Sometimes, however, the dye was even too expensive for royalty. Third-century Roman emperor Aurelian famously wouldn't allow his wife to buy a shawl made from Tyrian purple silk because it literally cost its weight in gold.

---

## A Teenager Changes Everything

For three thousand years, purple had belonged only to the powerful. Then, in 1856, an eighteen-year-old student in a London laboratory changed everything — by accident.

It wasn't until 1856 that a synthetic alternative to Tyrian purple was discovered, accidentally, by William Perkin, who was working as a student of August Wilhelm von Hofmann at the Royal College of Chemistry. He was trying to synthesise quinine, a natural product sought after for its antimalarial properties. While he didn't succeed in his goal, Perkin instead discovered how to make a purple dye — mauveine. He soon realised how lucrative his discovery could be, leaving his research behind to commercially manufacture the dye.

The colour's name was later changed to "mauve" in 1859, based on the French name for the purple mallow flower, with chemists calling the dye compound mauveine. The vibrant mauveine purple was derived from coal tar and made its creator a Fellow of the Royal Society and Royal Medallist.

Perkin developed an industrial process, built a factory, and produced the dye by the ton, so almost anyone could wear mauve. It was the first of a series of modern industrial dyes which completely transformed both the chemical industry and fashion.

It was so popular that purple became the height of fashion in Paris and London in the late 1850s and early 1860s, with even Queen Victoria choosing to wear a mauveine dress.

---

## Purple Today

The colour that had defined exclusivity for millennia was suddenly available to anyone. The economic impact of synthetic dyes was immediate and devastating for traditional dye industries. The Tyrian purple industry, already diminished, disappeared completely. Entire regions that had depended on natural dye production
